# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

tools.result:
# Ostrich

Ostrich is a dictionary compressor for small text records. It trains a dictionary per stream (`ostrich train`) and
needs the same dictionary to decompress.

final.result:
**Probably not, and nothing we have shows it would be.**

- **The benchmark doesn't cover our data.** Ostrich beat zstd -3 (4.1× vs 3.2×) on text logs under 1 MB. The wiki says binary payloads and files over 1 MB weren't tested. Our archives are protobuf-encoded binary frames of 40–300 MB, so those numbers don't apply.
- **It's built for a different job.** The README calls it "a dictionary compressor for small text records". Dictionaries help most with many small inputs. On large files, ordinary compressors like zstd build up that context themselves.
- **It adds work to run.** You need the same trained dictionary to decompress, so every dictionary has to be versioned and kept as long as the archives it was used on.

If you still want to consider it, run a quick test on a few real nightly files: Ostrich (dictionary trained on our frames) against zstd at a mid level, and against zstd `--long`. Compare compression ratio and speed. Unless Ostrich clearly wins there, I'd stay with zstd.
